cityEvents.title: The people occupy the Circus against Julianus
cityEvents.summary: Crowds jeered the new emperor in the Forum and then occupied the Circus Maximus, where they stayed a day and a night without food or water, calling on Niger in the East to come and save them.
cityEvents.locName: the Circus Maximus

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: Pertinax killed in the palace
cityEvents.summary: Two or three hundred praetorians marched on the palace; Pertinax met them in the halls and began to reason with them until a Tungrian soldier struck him. His head was carried on a spear back to the camp.
cityEvents.locName: the public halls of the Palatine palace

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: The empire auctioned at the Praetorian Camp
cityEvents.summary: Sulpicianus bid from inside the camp and Didius Julianus from outside the wall, shouting his offers and holding up his fingers; Julianus won at 25,000 sesterces a soldier and was led to the Forum and the Curia under guard.
cityEvents.locName: the walls of the Castra Praetoria

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: Funeral of Pertinax in the Forum
cityEvents.summary: Dio watched as a wax effigy of Pertinax lay on a platform built next to the marble Rostra under a canopy of gold and ivory; Severus read the eulogy and the effigy was carried to a three-storey pyre tower in the Campus Martius, from which an eagle flew up.
cityEvents.locName: a wooden platform beside the Rostra; pyre in the Campus Martius

cityEvents.title: Didius Julianus killed in the palace
cityEvents.summary: Deserted as Severus approached, Julianus was killed by a soldier in the palace after 66 days; his last words were 'What wrong have I done? Whom have I killed?'
cityEvents.locName: the palace on the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Septimius Severus enters Rome
cityEvents.summary: Severus came to the gates in armour, then changed into civilian dress and walked to the Capitol with his army; the city was garlanded and the people in white, but Dio found the soldiers' billeting in temples and porticoes frightening.
cityEvents.locName: from the gates to the Capitol

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: 'Alexamenos worships his god': the Palatine graffito
cityEvents.summary: On a wall of the imperial pages' building on the Palatine someone scratched a man raising his hand to a crucified figure with a donkey's head, captioned 'Alexamenos worships his god', the earliest known image of the crucifixion.
cityEvents.locName: the Paedagogium (Domus Gelotiana) on the SW Palatine above the Circus
cityEvents.note: Date c. 200, from the context; Tertullian mentions the donkey-headed slander.

cityEvents.title: Grain dole: tickets at the Porticus Minucia
cityEvents.summary: Holders of bronze grain tickets collected their monthly ration of free grain at one of the 45 arches of the Porticus Minucia Frumentaria, each assigned to a group of recipients on fixed days.
cityEvents.locName: the Porticus Minucia Frumentaria
cityEvents.note: Distribution system attested from Claudius into the 3rd century; year representative.

cityEvents.title: Mithraeum in a house under San Clemente
cityEvents.summary: In the courtyard of an insula beneath the later church of S. Clemente a mithraeum with benches and a bull-slaying altar was installed around 200, next to a house believed to be the titulus of Clement.
cityEvents.locName: the Mithraeum under S. Clemente

cityEvents.title: Consualia: the buried altar uncovered in the Circus
cityEvents.summary: The altar of Consus, kept underground near the first turning post of the Circus Maximus, was uncovered only on his festival days, when horses and mules were crowned and raced; Tertullian notes its inscription.
cityEvents.locName: the underground altar of Consus at the first metae of the Circus Maximus
cityEvents.note: Annual on 21 August; year representative.

cityEvents.title: A Mithraic initiation dated on the Aventine
cityEvents.summary: A painted inscription in the mithraeum beneath S. Prisca records a birth into the mysteries 'at first light' on 20 November in the consulship of the two Augusti, Severus and Antoninus, i.e. 202.
cityEvents.locName: the Mithraeum under S. Prisca on the Aventine

sources.r: VI (S. Prisca dipinti, Vermaseren and van Essen 1965)

cityEvents.title: Arch of Septimius Severus dedicated
cityEvents.summary: The senate and people dedicated a triple arch at the NW end of the Forum to Severus and his sons for the Parthian victories; after 212 Geta's name was erased from the attic inscription.
cityEvents.locName: the Arch of Septimius Severus beside the Rostra

cityEvents.title: The Septizodium screens the Palatine
cityEvents.summary: Severus built a three-storey colonnaded facade at the SE corner of the Palatine facing the Via Appia, so that travellers arriving from Africa would see his works first.
cityEvents.locName: the Septizodium at the SE corner of the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Money-changers and cattle dealers honour the Severans
cityEvents.summary: The argentarii and negotiantes boarii of the cattle market built a gate of marble at the entrance to the Forum Boarium beside S. Giorgio in Velabro, carving the imperial family; Geta, Plautianus and Plautilla were later chiselled out.
cityEvents.locName: the Arcus Argentariorum by S. Giorgio in Velabro

cityEvents.title: Severan Secular Games at the Tarentum
cityEvents.summary: Severus and Caracalla celebrated the Secular Games; the inscribed Acta, found by the Tiber, record the nocturnal sacrifices at the Tarentum and a hymn sung on the Palatine and Capitol by choirs of children.
cityEvents.locName: the Tarentum by the Tiber

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: Plautianus killed before the emperor
cityEvents.summary: Accused of plotting, the all-powerful prefect Plautianus was summoned to the palace and cut down in the presence of Severus and Julia Domna on Caracalla's orders; a hair from his beard was carried to Plautilla. His body was thrown into the street.
cityEvents.locName: a room of the Palatine palace

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: Septimius Severus' ashes laid in Hadrian's Mausoleum
cityEvents.summary: Severus died at York; his sons carried his ashes in a porphyry urn back to Rome, where they were placed in the Mausoleum of Hadrian after a funeral with an effigy.
cityEvents.locName: the Mausoleum of Hadrian

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: Geta murdered in his mother's arms
cityEvents.summary: Caracalla persuaded their mother Julia Domna to summon both sons to her rooms for a reconciliation; centurions burst in and killed Geta as he clung to her, her hand wounded. Caracalla rushed to the camp claiming he had escaped a plot.
cityEvents.locName: Julia Domna's apartments in the palace

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.note: Date given as 26 December 211 (some reconstructions 19 December).

cityEvents.title: Firemen's graffiti in the post of the Seventh Cohort
cityEvents.summary: In the excubitorium of the Seventh Cohort of vigiles in Trastevere, firemen scratched over a hundred dated graffiti between 215 and 245, thanking the genius of the post after their monthly sebaciaria duty of lighting the streets.
cityEvents.locName: the Excubitorium of the VII Cohort, Via della VII Coorte, Trastevere

cityEvents.title: Elagabalus breaks into the inner shrine of Vesta
cityEvents.summary: Elagabalus married the Vestal Aquilia Severa and, says the Historia Augusta, forced his way into the penus of Vesta, which only the Vestals and the chief priest might enter, to carry off what he thought was the Palladium to his own temple.
cityEvents.locName: the penus of the Temple of Vesta

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: The black stone of Elagabal paraded to its summer temple
cityEvents.summary: Each midsummer the conical stone of the sun god of Emesa rode in a gilded chariot from the Palatine temple to his suburban temple at Spes Vetus, the emperor running backward before it holding the reins, the road strewn with gold dust.
cityEvents.locName: from the Elagabalium on the Palatine (to the temple at Spes Vetus)

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: Elagabalus killed in the Praetorian Camp
cityEvents.summary: Mutinous praetorians killed Elagabalus and his mother Julia Soaemias in the camp, the emperor hiding in a latrine. Their heads were cut off and the bodies stripped and dragged through the city.
cityEvents.locName: the Castra Praetoria

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: Elagabalus' body thrown from the Pons Aemilius
cityEvents.summary: The body was dragged through the streets and around the Circus, pushed into a sewer which proved too small, and finally thrown into the Tiber from the Pons Aemilius with a weight attached so it would never be buried. He was nicknamed 'the dragged one'.
cityEvents.locName: the Pons Aemilius, after being dragged around the Circus Maximus

cityEvents.title: Pope Callistus killed in Trastevere
cityEvents.summary: The former slave and banker Callistus, who had run the Christian cemetery on the Via Appia, died in a riot in Trastevere; legend says he was thrown into a well. The church of S. Callisto marks the site.
cityEvents.locName: the well of S. Callisto near S. Maria in Trastevere
cityEvents.note: The Passio is late; the historical death in a riot is plausible but unverified.

cityEvents.title: Ulpian murdered in the palace
cityEvents.summary: After three days of street fighting between the people and the praetorians, who set houses on fire, the soldiers killed the jurist and prefect Ulpian at night in the palace, before the young emperor and his mother.
cityEvents.locName: the Palatine palace

cityEvents.title: Severus Alexander awards a public plot to the Christians
cityEvents.summary: When the Christians occupied a public place and the tavern-keepers claimed it, Alexander ruled that it was better for a god to be worshipped there in any fashion than for it to go to tavern-keepers. Tradition identified the site with S. Maria in Trastevere.
cityEvents.locName: a public plot in Trastevere (tradition: S. Maria in Trastevere)

cityEvents.title: Julius Africanus builds a library at the Pantheon
cityEvents.summary: The Christian scholar Julius Africanus wrote that he had designed the beautiful library in the Pantheon by the Baths of Alexander for the emperor.
cityEvents.locName: library at the Pantheon, beside the Baths of Nero/Alexander

cityEvents.title: Senators kill praetorians in the Curia
cityEvents.summary: When two or three praetorians came to the door of the senate house to listen, the senator Gallicanus and his friend Maecenas stabbed them at the altar of Victory. The people then besieged the praetorians in their camp.
cityEvents.locName: at the altar of Victory inside the Curia Iulia

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: The crowd demands a Gordian and he is shown on the Capitol
cityEvents.summary: As Pupienus and Balbinus went up to the Capitol, the people blocked their way demanding an emperor from Gordian's family; the 13-year-old grandson was fetched and named Caesar.
cityEvents.locName: the Capitol

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: Civil war in the streets: the camp besieged, the city burned
cityEvents.summary: The people attacked the Castra Praetoria and cut its water pipes; the praetorians sallied out, the people fought back from the rooftops and the soldiers set fire to the houses, burning a great part of the city.
cityEvents.locName: around the Castra Praetoria and the neighbouring streets

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: Pupienus and Balbinus dragged from the palace
cityEvents.summary: During the Capitoline games, while the people were at the shows, praetorians burst into the palace, stripped the two quarrelling emperors, dragged them through the streets toward the camp and killed them.
cityEvents.locName: from the palace through the streets toward the camp

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

cityEvents.title: Plotinus teaches in the house of Gemina
cityEvents.summary: Plotinus came to Rome at 40 and taught for 26 years in the house of the widow Gemina, where Porphyry, senators, physicians and women of the nobility attended; guardians left orphans and their property in his care.
cityEvents.locName: the house of Gemina (site unknown)
cityEvents.note: Porphyry gives no location. Marker placed nominally in the central Campus Martius; treat as unlocated.

cityEvents.title: Games for Rome's thousandth birthday
cityEvents.summary: Philip the Arab celebrated the millennium of the city with games in the Circus Maximus, using the elephants, elk, tigers, hippopotami and other animals gathered by Gordian III, and with theatrical shows in the Campus Martius.
cityEvents.locName: the Circus Maximus

cityEvents.title: A Mithraic cave under the Circus seating
cityEvents.summary: In the 3rd century the ground floor of a public building beside the Circus Maximus was turned into a mithraeum with a great relief of Mithras slaying the bull.
cityEvents.locName: the Mithraeum of the Circus Maximus (Via dell'Ara Massima di Ercole)
cityEvents.note: Year representative of its 3rd-century use.

cityEvents.title: Pope Fabian martyred; buried in the Crypt of the Popes
cityEvents.summary: Fabian was among the first victims of Decius' edict; his Greek epitaph, 'Fabian, bishop, martyr', survives in the Crypt of the Popes in the cemetery of Callixtus.
cityEvents.locName: the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of Callixtus

cityEvents.title: Sixtus II beheaded on his chair in the catacomb
cityEvents.summary: Under Valerian's edict soldiers surprised Bishop Sixtus II preaching seated in the cemetery of Callixtus and beheaded him with four deacons; Damasus later wrote verses for his tomb in the Crypt of the Popes.
cityEvents.locName: the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of Callixtus

cityEvents.title: Deacon Lawrence martyred and buried in the Ager Veranus
cityEvents.summary: Four days after Sixtus, the deacon Lawrence was executed; legend says he presented the poor as the church's treasure and was roasted on a gridiron. He was buried on the Via Tiburtina, where Constantine built a basilica.
cityEvents.locName: his tomb in the Ager Veranus on the Via Tiburtina (S. Lorenzo fuori le mura)
cityEvents.note: The gridiron legend is attested from Ambrose and Prudentius; the place of execution was later claimed by S. Lorenzo in Panisperna on the Viminal.

cityEvents.title: The Esquiline gate rededicated to Gallienus
cityEvents.summary: The prefect M. Aurelius Victor rebuilt the Augustan arch of the Porta Esquilina and dedicated it to Gallienus and Salonina 'whose unconquered courage is surpassed only by his piety'.
cityEvents.locName: the Arch of Gallienus (Porta Esquilina)

cityEvents.title: Plague kills 5000 a day in Rome
cityEvents.summary: In the worst year of the 'plague of Cyprian', the Historia Augusta claims 5000 people died in a single day in Rome, together with an earthquake and darkness over the city.
cityEvents.locName: the whole city

cityEvents.title: Aurelian begins the walls of Rome
cityEvents.summary: After the Juthungi reached Italy, Aurelian ordered a brick wall 19 km long around the city, the first new circuit since the Republic, built largely by the city guilds and completed under Probus.
cityEvents.locName: the Aurelian Wall (Porta Appia section shown)

cityEvents.title: Revolt of the mint workers on the Caelian
cityEvents.summary: Led by the official Felicissimus, the workers of the Rome mint, accused of debasing the coinage, rose in revolt and fought Aurelian's troops on the Caelian; 7000 soldiers are said to have died.
cityEvents.locName: the imperial mint (Moneta) on the Caelian near S. Clemente

cityEvents.title: Aurelian's triumph: Zenobia in golden chains
cityEvents.summary: Aurelian triumphed over Palmyra and the Gallic empire; Zenobia walked weighed down by jewels and gold chains carried by a jester, and the Gallic emperor Tetricus in trousers. The procession reached the Capitol only in the evening.
cityEvents.locName: triumphal route to the Capitol

cityEvents.title: Temple of Sol Invictus dedicated
cityEvents.summary: With Palmyrene spoils Aurelian built a great temple to the Unconquered Sun in the Campus Agrippae and created a new college of pontiffs of Sol; the god's festival fell on 25 December.
cityEvents.locName: the Temple of Sol in the Campus Agrippae (E Campus Martius)
cityEvents.note: Site disputed (under S. Silvestro in Capite or the Quirinal); placed in the Campus Agrippae.

cityEvents.title: Probus plants a forest in the Circus
cityEvents.summary: For his triumph Probus had soldiers uproot trees and replant them in the Circus Maximus, then released a thousand ostriches, deer, wild boars and sheep for the people to seize; lions and leopards were killed in the amphitheatre.
cityEvents.locName: the arena of the Circus Maximus, turned into a forest

cityEvents.title: The fire of Carinus burns the Forum
cityEvents.summary: A fire under Carinus burned the senate house, the Forum of Caesar, the Basilica Julia and the Graecostadium; Diocletian rebuilt the Curia in the form that survives.
cityEvents.locName: the Curia, Forum Iulium and Basilica Julia

cityEvents.title: Collapse in the Circus kills thousands
cityEvents.summary: The Chronograph of 354 records that under Diocletian the upper seating of the Circus Maximus collapsed and crushed 13,000 people.
cityEvents.locName: the seating of the Circus Maximus
cityEvents.note: Year within Diocletian's reign unknown; the figure may be corrupt.

cityEvents.title: Diocletian's vicennalia and the five columns
cityEvents.summary: Diocletian and Maximian celebrated twenty years of rule with a triumph in Rome; five honorific columns were set up behind the Rostra, the base of one carved with a sacrifice. Diocletian, irritated by the Roman crowd's liberties, left on 20 December.
cityEvents.locName: the Decennalia monument behind the Rostra

cityEvents.title: Agnes exposed under the arches of the stadium
cityEvents.summary: The young Agnes refused marriage and sacrifice; by tradition she was exposed in a brothel under the arches of Domitian's stadium, where her hair grew to cover her, and then killed. She was buried on the Via Nomentana.
cityEvents.locName: the arcades of the Stadium of Domitian (S. Agnese in Agone)
cityEvents.note: The brothel story is in the Passio and Prudentius; the stadium location is tradition.

cityEvents.title: Baths of Diocletian dedicated
cityEvents.summary: Maximian, returning from Africa, began the largest baths of Rome on the Viminal in Diocletian's name, clearing a whole neighbourhood; they were dedicated after the abdication of 305.
cityEvents.locName: the Baths of Diocletian on the Viminal

cityEvents.title: Maxentius proclaimed at the Praetorian Camp
cityEvents.summary: Angered by Galerius' plan to tax Rome and abolish the guard, the praetorians and people proclaimed Maximian's son Maxentius emperor in Rome.
cityEvents.locName: the Castra Praetoria

cityEvents.title: Fire in a temple and a massacre by Maxentius' soldiers
cityEvents.summary: When a temple of Fortuna caught fire and a soldier mocked the goddess, the crowd killed him; the soldiers rioted and massacred the people until Maxentius stopped them. The Temple of Venus and Roma was rebuilt by Maxentius after a fire.
cityEvents.locName: the Temple of Venus and Roma (probably the 'temple of Fortuna' of Zosimus)

cityEvents.title: Maxentius begins the Basilica Nova
cityEvents.summary: On the site of the burned Sacra Via warehouses Maxentius began a vaulted basilica on the scale of the imperial baths; Constantine finished it and set his colossal statue in the apse.
cityEvents.locName: the Basilica of Maxentius on the Velia

cityEvents.title: Circus and mausoleum of Maxentius on the Via Appia
cityEvents.summary: Maxentius built a palace, a circus with an obelisk of Domitian, and a dynastic mausoleum for his son Romulus, who died in 309, on the Via Appia.
cityEvents.locName: the Circus of Maxentius on the Via Appia

cityEvents.title: Constantine's colossal statue with the sign in his hand
cityEvents.summary: Eusebius says Constantine had a statue of himself holding the saving sign set up 'in the most public place in Rome'; the colossal marble head and hand found in 1486 in the apse of the Basilica Nova come from his giant seated statue.
cityEvents.locName: the W apse of the Basilica Nova

cityEvents.title: 'Constantine cannot be conquered!' shout the Circus crowd
cityEvents.summary: At the races for Maxentius' anniversary the crowd shouted that Constantine could not be beaten; alarmed, Maxentius consulted the Sibylline books, which foretold that 'the enemy of the Romans' would die, and marched out.
cityEvents.locName: the Circus Maximus

cityEvents.title: Maxentius drowns at the Milvian Bridge
cityEvents.summary: Routed at Saxa Rubra, Maxentius' army fled back across the Tiber; the pontoon bridge beside the stone Milvian Bridge collapsed and Maxentius, weighed down by armour, drowned. His body was recovered from the mud the next day.
cityEvents.locName: the Milvian Bridge and the pontoon bridge beside it

cityEvents.title: Constantine enters Rome with Maxentius' head
cityEvents.summary: Constantine entered by the Via Flaminia with Maxentius' head carried on a spear; the senate and people met him with joy, and he went to the palace on the Palatine.
cityEvents.locName: entry by the Porta Flaminia along the Via Lata
cityEvents.note: Whether he climbed to the Capitol to sacrifice is debated; the panegyrist is silent.

cityEvents.title: Constantine abolishes the Praetorian Guard
cityEvents.summary: Constantine dissolved the praetorians, who had fought for Maxentius, and dismantled the inner wall of their camp, ending three centuries of emperor-making from the Castra Praetoria.
cityEvents.locName: the Castra Praetoria

cityEvents.title: Constantine gives the Lateran to the bishop of Rome
cityEvents.summary: On the site of the razed barracks of the imperial horse guard, Constantine built the Basilica Constantiniana, Rome's cathedral, and gave the bishop the adjacent Lateran palace.
cityEvents.locName: the Lateran basilica on the barracks of the Equites Singulares

cityEvents.title: Council of bishops in the house of Fausta at the Lateran
cityEvents.summary: Pope Miltiades and nineteen bishops met in the house of Fausta on the Lateran to judge the Donatist dispute from Africa, the first church council held in an imperial residence.
cityEvents.locName: the Domus Faustae on the Lateran

cityEvents.title: Arch of Constantine dedicated for the decennalia
cityEvents.summary: The senate dedicated a triple arch beside the Colosseum to Constantine, who had freed the state from a tyrant 'by divine inspiration'; much of its sculpture was taken from monuments of Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus.
cityEvents.locName: the Arch of Constantine on the triumphal route by the Meta Sudans

cityEvents.title: Old St Peter's rises over the apostle's tomb
cityEvents.summary: Constantine levelled the Vatican hillside and buried a cemetery to build a five-aisled basilica with its apse over the 'trophy' of Peter; it was finished under his sons.
cityEvents.locName: Old St Peter's on the Vatican
cityEvents.note: Foundation date between c. 319 and 333.

cityEvents.title: Constantine refuses the procession to the Capitol
cityEvents.summary: On his last visit, for his vicennalia, Constantine declined to join the traditional procession up to the Capitol; Zosimus says the senate and people were enraged by the insult.
cityEvents.locName: the processional route up the Capitol

cityEvents.title: The legend of Constantine's baptism at the Lateran
cityEvents.summary: Later legend (the Actus Silvestri) held that Pope Silvester cured Constantine of leprosy and baptised him in the Lateran baptistery; in fact he was baptised on his deathbed near Nicomedia in 337.
cityEvents.locName: the Lateran baptistery

cityEvents.title: Constantina buried in her mausoleum on the Via Nomentana
cityEvents.summary: Constantine's daughter Constantina, who had founded the basilica of S. Agnese beside the martyr's tomb, was buried in the domed mausoleum next to it, with its vine-harvest mosaics and porphyry sarcophagus.
cityEvents.locName: the Mausoleum of Constantina (S. Costanza) on the Via Nomentana

cityEvents.title: Prefect Leontius faces down a riot at the Septizodium
cityEvents.summary: The city prefect Leontius ordered the arrest of a charioteer; the crowd rioted and burned the house of the prefect's office, and when a ringleader, Peter Valvomeres, harangued them, Leontius had him seized at the Septizodium, a much-frequented place, and flogged.
cityEvents.locName: the Septizodium at the SE corner of the Palatine

cityEvents.title: The great obelisk raised in the Circus Maximus
cityEvents.summary: Constantine's obelisk from Karnak, the tallest in the world, arrived by river barge and was hauled on rollers through the Porta Ostiensis to the Circus, where thousands of men raised it with a forest of masts and ropes on the spina.
cityEvents.locName: the spina of the Circus Maximus (obelisk now at the Lateran)

cityEvents.title: Constantius addresses the senate and the people
cityEvents.summary: Constantius spoke to the nobility in the Curia and to the people from the tribunal, was received in the palace and gave games, enjoying the banter of the plebs.
cityEvents.locName: the Curia and the Rostra

cityEvents.title: Constantius removes the altar of Victory
cityEvents.summary: During his visit Constantius had the altar of Victory taken out of the senate house, though he left the statue and the privileges of the priesthoods; Julian restored it.
cityEvents.locName: the altar of Victory in the Curia

cityEvents.title: Constantius II enters Rome like a statue
cityEvents.summary: Constantius rode in a golden carriage glittering with gems, surrounded by dragon standards and armoured cavalry, looking straight ahead without moving his head, bending only to pass under gates, as Ammianus describes in a famous scene.
cityEvents.locName: the triumphal entry along the Via Flaminia/Lata

cityEvents.title: Constantius stunned by the Forum of Trajan
cityEvents.summary: Touring the city, the emperor admired the Capitol, the baths, the Colosseum, the Pantheon, the Temple of Venus and Roma, the Temple of Peace, Pompey's theatre, the Odeum and the Stadium, but stood speechless in the Forum of Trajan. He said he would copy only the equestrian statue; the Persian prince Hormisdas replied: first build a stable like this one.
cityEvents.locName: the equestrian statue of Trajan in the Forum of Trajan

cityEvents.title: The legend of the snow on the Esquiline
cityEvents.summary: A medieval legend says the Virgin showed Pope Liberius and a patrician the site of her church by a summer snowfall on the Esquiline on 5 August; the Liberian basilica preceded S. Maria Maggiore.
cityEvents.locName: the Esquiline summit (S. Maria Maggiore)
cityEvents.note: Legend first attested in the Middle Ages.

cityEvents.title: Funeral of the prefect Junius Bassus at St Peter's
cityEvents.summary: The city prefect Junius Bassus died in office, 'newly baptised', and was buried near Peter's tomb in a carved sarcophagus whose biblical scenes are a masterpiece of early Christian sculpture.
cityEvents.locName: near the confession of Old St Peter's

cityEvents.title: Mob tries to burn Prefect Lampadius' house
cityEvents.summary: The vain prefect Lampadius, who requisitioned materials for his buildings without paying, so enraged the poor that they tried to burn his house near the Baths of Constantine with torches; he fled to the Milvian Bridge.
cityEvents.locName: Lampadius' house near the Baths of Constantine on the Quirinal

cityEvents.title: The Great Mother bathed in the Almo
cityEvents.summary: On 27 March the silver image of Cybele was carried in a cart out of the Porta Capena to the brook Almo, where its priest, robed in purple, washed it and its sacred objects; Ammianus records the rite still in the 4th century.
cityEvents.locName: the confluence of the Almo with the Tiber road outside the Porta Appia
cityEvents.note: Annual; year representative.

cityEvents.title: Fighting over the papacy at the Julian basilica
cityEvents.summary: On Liberius' death the deacon Ursinus was consecrated in the Julian basilica in Trastevere and Damasus at S. Lorenzo in Lucina; Damasus' partisans attacked the Julian basilica and fought in the streets for three days.
cityEvents.locName: the Julian basilica in Trastevere (S. Maria in Trastevere)

cityEvents.title: 137 dead in the Basilica of Sicininus
cityEvents.summary: Damasus' supporters stormed the Basilica of Sicininus, where the Ursinians had taken refuge, breaking in through the roof; Ammianus records 137 corpses found in a single day and drily notes the wealth of the Roman see.
cityEvents.locName: the Basilica of Sicininus on the Esquiline (Liberian basilica, near S. Maria Maggiore)
cityEvents.note: Usually identified with the Liberian basilica on the Esquiline, predecessor of S. Maria Maggiore.

cityEvents.title: Praetextatus restores the Porticus of the Twelve Gods
cityEvents.summary: The pagan city prefect Vettius Agorius Praetextatus restored the statues of the Dei Consentes in their portico below the Tabularium and demolished private buildings stuck onto temples.
cityEvents.locName: the Porticus Deorum Consentium on the Clivus Capitolinus

cityEvents.title: Damasus' verses in the Crypt of the Popes
cityEvents.summary: Pope Damasus restored the martyrs' tombs in the catacombs and placed verse inscriptions carved by Filocalus; in the Crypt of the Popes he declared he would have liked to be buried there but feared to disturb the saints.
cityEvents.locName: the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of Callixtus

cityEvents.title: Plebs burn the house of Symmachus in Trastevere
cityEvents.summary: The elder Symmachus, once city prefect, was rumoured to have said he would rather use his wine to slake lime than sell it cheap; the plebs burned his fine house in Trastevere and he left the city for a time.
cityEvents.locName: the house of L. Aurelius Avianius Symmachus in Trastevere
cityEvents.note: Ammianus dates it 'some time' after his prefecture (364-365); year approximate. The orator Symmachus was his son.

cityEvents.title: Taurobolia at the Phrygianum on the Vatican
cityEvents.summary: In the sanctuary of the Great Mother beside the Vatican circus, pagan aristocrats were drenched in the blood of a bull in the taurobolium and recorded it on altars dated between 295 and 390; they were found under St Peter's square.
cityEvents.locName: the Phrygianum near the Vatican circus (under Piazza S. Pietro)
cityEvents.note: Year representative of the dated altars of the 370s.

cityEvents.title: Jerome teaches scripture in Marcella's house on the Aventine
cityEvents.summary: Marcella's palace on the Aventine became a circle of ascetic noblewomen, Paula, Asella and others, who studied Hebrew and scripture with Jerome while he served Pope Damasus.
cityEvents.locName: the house of Marcella on the Aventine
cityEvents.note: The house is unlocated on the Aventine.

cityEvents.title: Augustine teaches rhetoric in Rome
cityEvents.summary: Augustine came from Carthage because Roman students were said to be orderly, fell ill in the house of a Manichaean, and found that his pupils cheated him by moving en masse to another teacher before paying fees. In 384 he left for the chair in Milan.
cityEvents.locName: a rhetoric school in Rome (site unknown)
cityEvents.note: No location given. Marker in the Forum of Trajan, where public recitation and teaching are attested in late antiquity (Venantius Fortunatus, Carm. 3.18, 7.8).

cityEvents.title: Symmachus pleads for the altar of Victory
cityEvents.summary: As city prefect, Symmachus asked Valentinian II to restore the altar of Victory to the senate house: 'We cannot attain to so great a mystery by one road.' Ambrose of Milan's replies prevailed.
cityEvents.locName: the altar of Victory in the Curia

cityEvents.title: Theodosius in Rome; Pacatus' panegyric in the senate
cityEvents.summary: Theodosius entered Rome after defeating Magnus Maximus, walked through the city as a private citizen visiting the houses of senators, and heard the Gallic orator Pacatus praise him in the senate house.
cityEvents.locName: the Curia

sources.w: On the Sixth Consulship of Honorius

cityEvents.title: Serena takes the necklace from the statue of Rhea
cityEvents.summary: Visiting the temple of the Great Mother on the Palatine after Theodosius' victory, Stilicho's wife Serena took the necklace from the goddess's statue and put it on; an old Vestal cursed her, and Zosimus saw her strangling in 408 as the curse fulfilled.
cityEvents.locName: the Temple of Magna Mater on the Palatine

cityEvents.title: Pammachius feasts the poor in the atrium of St Peter's
cityEvents.summary: In memory of his dead wife Paulina, the senator Pammachius gave a great banquet for the poor of Rome in the courtyard of St Peter's, a scene Paulinus of Nola describes with the crowds filling the atrium.
cityEvents.locName: the atrium of Old St Peter's

cityEvents.title: Honorius doubles the height of the walls
cityEvents.summary: Under the threat of Alaric's invasion, Stilicho had the Aurelian Wall raised to nearly twice its height and the gates rebuilt with towers, recorded in inscriptions over the Porta Tiburtina and Porta Praenestina.
cityEvents.locName: the Porta Tiburtina with its Honorian inscription

sources.w: On the Sixth Consulship of Honorius

cityEvents.title: Prudentius at the shrine of Hippolytus
cityEvents.summary: The Spanish poet Prudentius describes the crowds pouring out of the city on 13 August to the underground shrine of the martyr Hippolytus by the Via Tiburtina, its walls painted with his martyrdom.
cityEvents.locName: the catacomb of S. Ippolito on the Via Tiburtina
cityEvents.note: Prudentius visited Rome c. 401-403.

cityEvents.title: Crowds cross the Tiber for the feast of Peter and Paul
cityEvents.summary: On 29 June, Prudentius writes, the whole city streams across the Tiber to Peter's basilica on the Vatican and along the road to Paul's on the Via Ostiensis, the pope celebrating at both in one day.
cityEvents.locName: the Pons Aelius on the way to St Peter's

cityEvents.title: The monk Telemachus killed in the arena; gladiators abolished
cityEvents.summary: Theodoret says the eastern monk Telemachus leapt into the arena to separate fighting gladiators and was stoned to death by the angry spectators; Honorius then ended gladiatorial combat.
cityEvents.locName: the arena of the Flavian Amphitheatre
cityEvents.note: Date c. 404; Theodoret does not name the building.

cityEvents.title: Melania cannot sell her house on the Caelian
cityEvents.summary: Melania the Younger and Pinianus, giving away their vast fortune, could find no buyer rich enough for their house on the Caelian; after the sack of 410 it sold for a trifle, part of it burned.
cityEvents.locName: the Domus Valeriorum on the Caelian (by the Lateran)

cityEvents.title: Honorius' consular triumph in Rome
cityEvents.summary: For his sixth consulship Honorius entered Rome with Stilicho after the victories over Alaric; Claudian describes the crowds on the Pincian and the Milvian Bridge and the young emperor received on the Palatine.
cityEvents.locName: the entry by the Via Flaminia to the Palatine

sources.w: On the Sixth Consulship of Honorius

cityEvents.title: Arch of Arcadius, Honorius and Theodosius by the Pons Aelius
cityEvents.summary: The senate dedicated an arch at the Campus Martius end of the Pons Aelius to the three emperors for the defeat of the Goths at Pollentia and Verona.
cityEvents.locName: the arch at the left-bank end of the Pons Aelius
